title: Special Effects: A Short History
summary: Josh and Chuck open with lawn-mower banter, then cover the history and techniques of movie special effects. They sort effects into practical, in-camera, and post-production categories, and trace early tricks from Alfred Clark's 1895 stop trick and Georges Méliès through matte painting (Norman Dorn's original negative matte painting), rear and front projection, the Williams process and optical printers, blue and green screen, and motion control (Dykstra Flex on Star Wars). They discuss stop-motion pioneers (Willis O'Brien, Ray Harryhausen), makeup artists (Lon Chaney, Dick Smith, Rick Baker, Stan Winston, Tom Savini), Millicent Patrick's uncredited Gill Man design, and the move to CGI, motion capture (Gollum, WETA, ILM), and de-aging. A listener email about roofing and rooftop solar panels closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and tour dates
segments.summary: Tour dates in Orlando and New Orleans are announced, followed by off-topic chat about hats, lawn mowers, and the film The Changeling.

segments.title: Overview of special effects categories
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce special effects and sort them into practical, in-camera, and post-production effects, giving examples like prosthetics and fake fire.

segments.title: In-camera effects and early basis of trickery
segments.summary: Examples of in-camera effects such as slow motion, fast motion, stop-motion animation, and double exposure from still photography, which gave early filmmakers a basis of trickery.

segments.title: Early pioneers: Alfred Clark and Georges Méliès
segments.summary: Alfred Clark's 1895 stop trick in The Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots is described. Georges Méliès, called the father of special effects, discovered the substitution splice by accident in Paris in 1896 and made A Trip to the Moon in 1902.

segments.title: Matte painting, rear projection, and shaken car shots
segments.summary: Matte painting is explained, including original negative matte painting pioneered by Norman Dorn, James Cameron's early matte painting job on Escape from New York, and examples in Mary Poppins and Superman. Rear and front projection are covered, along with the car-shaking technique used for driving scenes.

segments.title: Green screen, blue screen, and the Williams process
segments.summary: Early green screen used sodium vapor lights. The Invisible Man (1933) used black-screen filming, which is the Williams process, relying on an optical printer. Blue screen gave way to green screen.

segments.title: Optical printers and compositing
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain how an optical printer projects and re-films separate elements to combine them into one shot.

segments.title: Motion control cameras and Star Wars
segments.summary: Motion control cameras repeat precise camera moves. Star Wars used them, along with an optical printer, to make static models appear to move, with John Dykstra's Dykstraflex rig.

segments.title: Jurassic Park and Academy Award history
segments.summary: Jurassic Park's raptor kitchen scene mixed puppets, costumes, animatronics, and CGI. The Abyss is discussed as an early CGI Oscar winner.

segments.title: Wire removal and Forrest Gump
segments.summary: Wire removal is discussed, including the Mad Max and Forrest Gump examples.

segments.title: Industry changes and return to practical effects
segments.summary: John Dykstra expresses tiredness with excessive spectacle. Josh predicts a return to practical effects, and Chuck notes that indie filmmakers now have cheap computer tools.

segments.title: Key effects artists: stop motion and makeup pioneers
segments.summary: Lon Chaney, Willis O'Brien, Ray Harryhausen, Millicent Patrick (uncredited Gill Man designer), Dick Smith, Rick Baker, Stan Winston, and Tom Savini are discussed. King Kong (1933) took about seven weeks for its fight scene.

segments.title: Studios, motion capture, and first CGI
segments.summary: ILM and WETA are discussed, with motion capture explained and Gollum cited. Young Sherlock Holmes is claimed as the first full CGI character, and The Wrath of Khan and Looker are noted as early CGI milestones.

segments.title: Modern CGI, de-aging, and color grading
segments.summary: De-aging in The Irishman and Gemini Man is discussed, as are digital color grading in O Brother, Where Art Thou? and deepfakes.

segments.title: Movie Crush plug and The Matrix
segments.summary: Chuck plugs his podcast Movie Crush. Josh mentions an upcoming episode on The Matrix, and the hosts briefly discuss the film and its cast.

segments.title: Listener email on roofs and solar panels
segments.summary: A listener who works as a roofer writes that people should check the age of their roof before installing solar panels, since reroofing with panels installed costs considerably more. The hosts read it as a PSA.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck invites listeners to get in touch through the website and email. The episode closes with the iHeartRadio credit.
